summary: Maryland has no smoke-alarm requirement that is triggered by selling or transferring a home, but it does require every existing home in the state to have been brought up to the current alarm standard by January 1, 2018 - so a compliant house should already be compliant on closing day.
alarmType: At least one alarm in each sleeping area, plus, under the upgrade rule, at least one on every level including the basement (unoccupied attics, garages and crawl spaces excepted). Alarms must be AC-primary powered with battery backup, with two exceptions: one- and two-family homes built before July 1, 1975 may use battery alarms, and a battery alarm may be used in a brand-new location where no alarm existed before. Where a battery alarm is allowed, it must be a sealed, tamper-resistant unit with a silence/hush button running on a long-life battery, which the statute defines as a nonrechargeable, nonreplaceable battery good for at least 10 years. Alarms must meet UL 217 and be installed per NFPA 72. If two or more alarms are required in a unit built on or after January 1, 1989, they must be interconnected so one sounding sets off all of them. Homes built on or after July 1, 2013 need an alarm in every sleeping room, outside the sleeping rooms, and on every level, all AC powered with battery backup and interconnected.
coAlarms: Maryland's CO alarm law is narrower than its smoke alarm law and also has no sale trigger. It reaches only a dwelling that burns fossil fuel for heat, ventilation, hot water or a clothes dryer AND was newly built under a permit issued on or after January 1, 2008, plus hotels, lodging and rooming houses, and rental units. An older owner-occupied house being sold is not covered. Where it applies, a CO alarm goes in a central spot outside each sleeping area; rental units since April 1, 2018 need one outside each separate sleeping area and on every level including the basement. The alarm must be AC-wired with battery backup (rentals and hotels may instead use a sealed tamper-resistant 10-year battery unit or a monitored unit). Combination smoke/CO alarms are allowed if they meet UL 217 and 2034, or UL 268 and 2075.
certification: Nobody has to inspect or sign off at sale. Enforcement is by the State Fire Marshal, a county or municipal fire marshal, a fire chief, the Baltimore City Fire Department or another authority having jurisdiction, and it works by complaint and installation order - the fire marshal can order a missing alarm installed and the owner has 5 days to comply. The owner is responsible for installation, repair, maintenance and replacement. Knowingly violating the subtitle is a misdemeanor carrying up to 10 days in jail or a $1,000 fine. Separately, failure to comply cannot be used as a policy defense to deny a property insurance claim.
citation: Md. Code, Public Safety §§ 9-101 to 9-109 (smoke alarms; § 9-104(d) is the upgrade/10-year rule, § 9-106 enforcement and responsibility, § 9-106.1 retail sale of battery alarms); Md. Code, Public Safety §§ 12-1101 to 12-1104 (carbon monoxide alarms)
notVerified: No sale- or transfer-specific smoke or CO alarm requirement exists in Maryland statute as far as this research found. The full text of Md. Public Safety §§ 9-101 through 9-109 and §§ 12-1101 through 12-1104 was read on mgaleg.maryland.gov and none of it is triggered by sale, transfer of title or settlement. The Office of the State Fire Marshal's own explanation of the law lists the upgrade triggers as alarm over 10 years old, alarm failure, change of tenant, a building permit for an addition or renovation, and January 1, 2018 at the latest - sale is not among them. Treat any claim that Maryland requires alarms 'at sale' as unsupported unless a more specific source is found.

The Maryland Real Property Article (seller disclosure/disclaimer form under Real Property § 10-702) was NOT examined. A seller disclosure duty about alarm condition, if one exists, would live there rather than in the Public Safety Article.

Local requirements were not researched. Md. Public Safety § 9-102(e) expressly lets local jurisdictions adopt stricter smoke alarm rules, so an individual county or Baltimore City could impose something at sale. Baltimore County and Anne Arundel County both publish their own smoke alarm pages that were not read.

mgaleg.maryland.gov statute pages do not display an amendment history, so the date each section was last amended was not verified. § 9-102(c)(2) references a requirement beginning July 31, 2025 and § 9-106.1 one effective October 1, 2018, which show the subtitle has been amended at least that recently, but the exact session law years were not confirmed.
The State Fire Prevention Code and the NFPA 72 / NFPA 101 / NFPA 720 standards the statute incorporates by reference were not read.
